prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

It’s my belief that every man Should do his share of work, And in our economic plan No citizen should shirk. That in return each one should get His meed of fold and food, And feel that all his toil and sweat Is for the common good. It’s my belief that every chap Should have an equal start, And there should be no handicap To hinder his depart; That there be fairness in the fight, And justice in the race, And every lad should have the right To win his proper place. It’s my belief that people should Be neither rich nor poor; That none should suffer servitude, And all should be secure. That wealth is loot, and rank is rot, And foul is class and clan; That to succeed a man may not Exploit his brother man. It’s my belief that heritage And usury are wrong; That each should win a worthy wage And sing an honest song .... Not one like this — for though I rue The wrong of life, I flout it. Alas! I’m not prepared to do A goddam thing about it.

outputs.L1:
It’s my belief that every man  
Should do his share of work,  
And in our economic plan  
No citizen should shirk;  
That, in return, each one should get  
His meed of fold and food,  
And feel that all his toil and sweat  
Are for the common good.

It’s my belief that every chap  
Should have an equal start,  
And there should be no handicap  
To hinder his depart;  
That there be fairness in the fight  
And justice in the race,  
And every lad should have the right  
To win his proper place.

It’s my belief that people should  
Be neither rich nor poor;  
That none should suffer servitude,  
And all should be secure;  
That wealth is loot, and rank is rot,  
And foul are class and clan;  
That, to succeed, a man may not  
Exploit his brother man.

It’s my belief that heritage  
And usury are wrong;  
That each should win a worthy wage  
And sing an honest song...

Not one like this—for though I rue  
The wrongs of life, I flout it.

outputs.L2:
I hold that every person ought  
To carry their fair load,  
And no one in society  
Should dodge the work they owe.  
In turn, each worker should receive  
Enough for food and home,  
And know their effort benefits  
The welfare of us all.  

I think that everyone deserves  
The same chance at the start,  
With no unfair obstruction placed  
To keep them from their path.  
The contest should be equitable,  
The race governed by right,  
So every youth may earn the place  
That properly is theirs.  

I believe no one should possess  
Too much or lack the least;  
All people should be safe from want,  
And none should live enslaved.  
Great fortunes are stolen goods, high status is absurd,  
And social castes and factions are corrupt;  
No person has the right to rise  
By using someone else.  

I also think inherited wealth  
And lending for interest are wrong;  
Each person should earn decent pay  
And voice an honest song—  
Though not a song like this one here.  
I grieve at life’s injustice  
And boldly speak against it, yet,  
Regrettably, I have no intention  
Of doing one damn thing to change it.
outputs.L3:
Every person should contribute a fair share of work and labor to promote the common good. In return for these efforts, everyone should receive adequate food, fair compensation, personal security, and the basic necessities of a dignified life. All people should begin with equal opportunities, face no unjust disadvantages, and have a genuine chance to succeed through their abilities and efforts.

A just society should therefore reject extreme wealth and poverty, inherited privilege, rigid class divisions, and every form of exploitation. No one should prosper by taking unfair advantage of others, nor should a person’s social position be determined by birth. Yet despite recognizing and condemning these injustices, the speaker acknowledges a personal contradiction: an unwillingness to take meaningful action to challenge or change them.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents an expansive vision of social justice through a rhythmic catalogue of socialist ideals. It calls for equality among people, the fair distribution of labor, genuine access to opportunity, and economic security for all. In this imagined society, no one would be condemned to poverty while others enjoy the rewards of collective work. Instead, people would share both responsibilities and benefits, and every individual would have the freedom to live without exploitation, deprivation, or dependence on the arbitrary power of the wealthy.

The poem’s catalogue-like structure reinforces the breadth of this vision. By listing one principle after another, the speaker creates a sense of momentum and moral certainty. The regular rhythm makes the demands sound almost like a manifesto, a public speech, or a political chant. Each ideal appears reasonable and humane, and their accumulation suggests that injustice is not a single isolated problem but a system involving work, wealth, power, and opportunity. The form therefore mirrors the poem’s political content: the repeated statements gather force and seem to build toward a call for social transformation.

However, the ending abruptly undermines this apparent commitment. After expressing support for so many admirable reforms, the speaker confesses that he will do nothing to help bring them about. This final admission transforms the poem into a satire of passive moralizing. The speaker is willing to praise equality and condemn exploitation in theory, but he refuses the effort, sacrifice, or risk required to challenge injustice in practice. His ideals become a form of self-flattery rather than a basis for meaningful change.

The poem therefore distinguishes between professed belief and genuine conviction. It suggests that it is easy to approve of justice in the abstract, especially when doing so demands nothing personally. Yet social and economic wrongs cannot be corrected by sympathetic words alone. The ironic ending exposes the hypocrisy of those who present themselves as morally enlightened while remaining inactive. Ultimately, the poem argues that principles acquire value only when they lead to action: without participation, solidarity, and practical commitment, even the noblest political ideals remain empty.
outputs.L5:
### Should, And, That

“Should,” “and,” and “that” are small words with important roles in English. **Should** expresses advice, expectation, or responsibility: “We should help others.” **And** connects words or ideas: “Kindness and patience matter.” **That** can identify something or introduce a statement: “I believe that everyone should be treated fairly.”

Together, these words help us express clear and connected thoughts: “We should remember that respect and understanding can bring people together.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a rhyming satirical poem about a man who professes socialism, equality, fair wages, and opposition to inherited wealth but refuses to take action.
counterfactuals.output:
He praised the worker, fist held high,  
And cursed the gilded towers nearby.  
“Fair wages now! Let fortunes fall!  
The wealth of Earth belongs to all!”

He toasted Marx with vintage wine,  
Then asked which stocks were set to climb.  
He loathed inherited estates—  
Except, of course, his uncle’s gates.

“Equality!” he’d loudly cry,  
While household staff went bustling by.  
“The rich must pay their proper share”—  
Then moved his funds to Delaware.

He swore each strike was just and right,  
Provided none disturbed his flight.  
He backed reform with brave applause,  
But never time, or cash, or cause.

“Comrades,” he’d say, “we must begin!”  
Then wait for someone else to win.  
For though his principles were grand,  
They never quite reached either hand.

And so he fought, from chair and phone,  
For bread and rights—and left alone  
Each deed that might incur a cost:  
A hero where no sleep was lost.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Produce a humorous, old-fashioned verse criticizing hypocrisy: the narrator passionately condemns class, poverty, exploitation, and usury, then confesses that he is unwilling to help change society.
counterfactuals.output:
### **The Ballad of Amos Aloof**

Oh, fie upon the gilded great  
Who dine from silver platters,  
While Want sits shivering at the gate  
In most unseemly tatters!  
The lord has ten embroidered coats,  
The hind but half a trouser;  
Such crimes, I cry, inflame my notes—  
Pray, do not rouse the mouser.

Down, down with Class! Let station fall!  
Let dukes embrace the ditcher!  
Let equal portions bless us all—  
(Though mine should be the richer.)  
Curse every mill whose grinding wheel  
Makes pale the weaver’s daughter;  
I deeply for her hardship feel—  
But shan’t subscribe a quarter.

And woe betide the usurer,  
That lean, percentish sinner,  
Who takes the poor man’s cupboard bare  
To furnish forth his dinner!  
May Heaven roast his flinty soul  
And confiscate his carriage—  
I’d lead reform from pole to pole,  
Were action not so garish.

“Come, march!” my earnest neighbours plead;  
“Come, aid the grand solution!”  
I answer, “Friends, I quite concede  
The need for revolution.  
Yet Thursday is my day for tea,  
And Friday, rain or weather;  
So overthrow society—  
But kindly go together.”
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
